subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OP CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
The amendment does not
change the general principle I was discussing at the close of the last sitting of the committee. At that time I dealt with the fundamental principle that it-he control of the bank should be directed to dominate, namely the issue of currency and credit in terms of public need.
By the amendment the government is given control over the board of directors, but unfortunately the directors do not control the bank. In proof of that fact I should1 like to draw the attention of the committee to certain provisions in the Bank of Canada Act. First I direct the attention of hon. members to section 8, which states that the governor, deputy governor and assistant deputy governor shall each be appointed as in the act provided for a term of several years. They are to be appointed by the governor in council. The actual clauses of the act which define and establish the control of the affairs of the bank are sections 13 and 14, the first of which reads as follows:
13.	(1) There shall be an executive committee of the board, consisting of the governor, the deputy governor and one director selected by the board.
Then subsection 3 provides:
The executive committee shall be competent to deal with any matter within the competence of the board but every decision of the committee shall be submitted to the board at its next meeting.
14.	No action or decision of the board of directors, or of the executive committee, shall have any effect unless the same is concurred in by the governor, or in his absence or incapacity, the deputy governor.
As a matter of fact, these sections place the actual control of the administration, of the bank's affairs in the hands of the executive committee, two of whom are appointed by governor in council, and who hold office at the will of parliament. Parliament could dismiss

them by amending the act., or by repealing the act, just as has been done in connection with the trustees of the Gainadlian National Railways.
It does not matter how many members there are on the board of directors, the board of directors have nothing whatever to say about the administration of the affairs of the bank unless what they suggest is concurred in by the governor, who along with the deputy governor, is under the control of parlia-liament because parliament may dismiss or remove them from office. They form the majority of an executive committee which today has full control over the administration of the bank's affairs. They are superior to the board of directors and, consequently, the board of directors is not a group of men the majority of whom can dominate or control the affairs of the bank. A majority of the board of directors appointed by the governments' shareholders means absolutely nothing.
During the course of my remarks yesterday the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) asked this question: What would you do with the $724,000,000 that the Bank of Canada now has the power under the act to issue; would you issue that money as a means of putting people to work? In answer to that, I should like to say that if proper control were established in the Bank of Canada it should be such control that the government, the Bank of Canada, the chartered banks and the financial institutions could get together to create the means of financing those sound public works, national, provincial and municipal, which would be the means of eliminating unemployment and putting people to work at work that is needed to be done. Of course, you would not use the legal tender currency of the Bank of Canada; you would be able to make arrangements with the chartered banks and the financial institutions by which short term treasury bills at minimum cost would be issued to carry on this work.
It may be said that it is impossible to do that, but I want to point out that that is exactly what is being done by the federal reserve board in the United States. A great deal of the money which has been used to put people in that country to work has been simply the credit of the member banks of the United States federal reserve system which has been issued for the use of the government as loans bearing interest rates as low as one-tenth of one per cent. I quite agree that the federal reserve system is far from perfection. I do not suggest for one moment that the mere fact that under the act, with the reserves of gold that the Bank of Canada

Bank oj Canada
has available, a sufficient number of Bank of Canada bills to support upwards of $7,000,000,000 of bank credit can be issued, would afford a complete panacea for all the social and economic and political ills of the Dominion of Canada. What I do say is that we have the necessary credit machinery now established and if it can be controlled so that currency and credit can be issued in terms of public need, there would be no necessity for the terrible conditions which now exist in Montreal, for the bankrupt conditions now continuing in Alberta and for the plight of our cities from one end of this dominion to the other.
The reason why the government should establish complete ownership of and control over the Bank of Canada is simply because it is not a bank of issue solely for the service of the chartered banks. It should be established as a bank of issue and as a national bank serving the public interests nationally, provincially and municipally, through which bank issues of public money and public credit for expenditure by national, provincial and municipal governments could be brought under proper and regulated control. We do not need to go to the senate or to the British parliament for an amendment to the British North America Act in order to establish a system under which coordination, regulation and control of public expenditures by all political executives throughout the Dominion of Canada could be brought within the control of the national authority.
There is one other matter which I should like to mention, a matter which has been raised time and again. If we issue through our Bank of Canada the money necessary to finance, without the appalling interest costs that public moneys now have to pay, what would happen to our international exchange? How could that be sustained? I hope I appreciate that when one advocates a substantial change in an existing system, he should have some authority which is recognized as one speaking with knowledge. In this regard, I think the statement of Mr. Beaudry Leman, who was once President of the Canadian Bankers' Association and who is the head of one of our largest French Canadian banks, the Banque Canadienne Nationale, should be accepted. This gentleman filed a report which was not in concurrence with the reports of the English members of the Macmillan commission. Mr. Leman said:
Certain features of the suggested constitution of a central bank for Canada, should one be established ultimately, appear unacceptable and do not afford sufficient safeguards in regard to currency and monetary matters: (a) In addition to minor objections to a
number of clauses, notably to clause No. 8, which fails to differentiate between the ratio of deposits to be made in the central bank in respect of notice deposits on the one hand, and of demand deposits on the other, I do take strong exception to clause No. 13, which states that:	"The bank should maintain a
proportion of 25 per cent in gold and foreign exchange against its outstanding note issue and sight liabilities." This clause makes no provision for the holding by the bank of a minimum amount of gold, or of a minimum percentage of gold against liabilities, nor does it even provide that the foreign exchange held by the bank should be convertible into gold. It will be argued that the governors and directors of the central bank would exercise their authority with prudence, skill and discretion. and that, in practice, sufficient gold would be held in reserve, and that a judicious choice would be made of the foreign exchange held by the central bank. The clause appears all the more surprising at a time when no one can have forgotten what befell the sterling, French franc and United States dollar exchange. Shall the currency of Canada he exposed to the uncertainties which might arise from possible errors of judgment on the part of the central bank? Can we be so sanguine as to hope that those who will guide the central bank and determine its policies will be men of such calibre that they will be at all times above human frailty, and will outclass in ability and foresight the bankers now at the head of the oldest and most powerful central banking institutions in the world? (b) Paragraph No. 207 of our report acknowledges that the state "must necessarily retain ultimate sovereignty in matters affecting the currency," and I find it difficult to reconcile this fundamental consideration with the power proposed to be given to the central bank under clause No. 13. Surely the parliament of Canada would not confer upon any organization, much less one privately owned, the right, implied in this clause, to strip this country bare of every ounce or dollar of gold and ship it abroad, holding in exchange, as the sole backing of the currency of Canada and as the bulk of its cash reserves, a claim on some inconvertible outside or foreign currency.
The mere suggestion that such a situation might develop would be more than enough to wreck the credit standing of this country and undermine the confidence which long years of faithful and sound banking have brought to Canadian institutions both public and private.
I read that for this reason. Here we have from the pen of one of Canada's outstanding bankers a statement condemning the methods, the practices and the securities which exist for the stabilizing of our international exchange under the present Bank of Canada Act. In Great Britain they did not rely, or they found it impossible to rely upon the Bank of England for the stabilization of the pound sterling after the collapse of 1931. When the stabilization fund was set up it was not set up in the Bank of England. The fund was administered by the Chancellor of the Exchequer and the power of the nation was given in an inflationary issue of sterling totalling $1,750,000,000. That power was given to the Chancellor of the Exchequer to
Bank oj Canada

go into the money markets of the world to maintain the value of the pound sterling as a function of the British government. In that regard the same gentleman, Mr. Leman, has this to say:
It is difficult to conceive how and to what extent, under present conditions, a monetary system can be placed beyond political influence. In Great Britain, the government, and not the Bank of England, provided the funds to establish and operate the "equalization fund" in which some seventeen hundred millions of dollars are now involved; in the United States the provisions of the statutes governing the activities of the federal reserve banks have been profoundly altered, this year, to conform with the policies and exigencies of the government of the United States; in Prance, only last year, parliament voted some ninety millions of dollars to guarantee the losses sustained by the Bank of France in pursuance of the instructions issued by the government of France to the effect that credit balances were not to be withdrawn from Great Britain; these instances of what is happening in the wealthiest and most powerful countries in the world, each provided with a central bank, should offer sufficient evidence as to what must inevitably happen in countries of lesser financial importance.
What has happened sipce Mr. Leman as a member of the Royal Commission on Banking and Currency issued this statement? Great Britain has maintained successfully the operation of the stabilization fund, which Mr. Winston Churchill, in the British House of Commons, the other day described as "the secret processes" that had' successfully taken the place of the very kind of system which has been set up in the Bank of Canada. What has happened in the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

That is quite right.
[Mr. McGeer.J

subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OP CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
Then you are operating
under the Bank of Canada unless you are doing something yourself. Of course, I do not profess to know what secret processes are going on in Canada any more than I profess to know what secret processes are going on in England, but I know that in the United States the federal reserve bank has nothing to do with the stabilization fund. It is a function of the Treasury department conducted by the Secretary of the Treasury, Mr. Morgenthau, as a personal duty and a personal obligation. When you come to the question whether or not you can maintain the internal economy of the country oy managing your domestic currency without interfering with the value of the buying power of your unit of exchange in world markets, I think you come to the question- whether or not you can manage your domestic currency from a central bank like the Bank of Canada and your international buying power in world markets as a direct function of the government itself through the Department of Finance, with nothing more -than those connecting links that exist and must of necessity exist between the Department of Finance in all its activities and the Bank of Canada. But let me say further that when it comes to the question of maintaining the international value of the unit of exchange it is less a monetary matter than it is a trade matter. If our government, as the government of Great Britain has done, can successfully set up the means of regulating its international trade, its transactions in international credit and currency, its transactions in tourist trade, so that we can maintain a balance or something close to a balance of trade internationally, then we shall have no difficulty in maintaining the value of our Canadian dollar in those countries with which we intend to trade. But those who confuse domestic currency-that is, silver coins or copper coins or nickel coins and paper currencies such as silver certificates or bank notes or bank deposits transferable by cheque-with international currency, are developing in their minds a difficulty and a hindrance to internal prosperity and progress which really does not exist. There are two real problems; one is international exchange and the buying power of our unit of exchange abroad, and the other is putting into circulation the domestic currency and credit that will permit our people to produce and distribute wealth in their own service, and producing surpluses which they can use in exchange with people in foreign lands for the things that will make for a higher

Bank of Canada
standard of living of our people in our own country. What I am putting forward is not new.

subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OP CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OP CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
Well, it is not new as
far as other countries are concerned but it has yet to be adopted in Canada. The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George asked me what I would do if I were Prime Minister of Canada. One of the first things I would do would be to convert the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) to some of the things that are now fairly current. For instance, one of the first acts would be to get a full appreciation of. what the British Macmillan report meant when it said to the British government in 1913, in section 280:
The monetary system of this country must be a managed system. It is not advisable, or indeed practicable, to regard our monetary system as an automatic system grinding out the right result by the operation of natural forces aided by a few maxims of general application and some well worn rules of thumb. The major objectives of a sound monetary policy-for example, the maintenance of the parity of the foreign exchanges without unnecessary disturbance to domestic business, the avoidance of the credit cycle, and the stability of the price level-cannot be attained except by the constant exercise of knowledge, judgment and authority, by individuals placed in a _ position of unchallengeable independence, with great resources and every technical advice at their disposition.
I think we have, in the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, an exceptionally fine group of fairly well trained men who, with the limited resources at their disposal, are able to present a remarkable but not by any means complete picture whereby it is possible for us to see where we are going in this Dominion of Canada. But when we have statements presented as we did1 in the budget that with ouir sales of gold abroad we had approximately a favourable balance of trade of 8435,000,000, one wonders why this nation should have shipped' abroad to exchange for the mom-convertible paper currency of a foreign nation or a non-convertible bank deposit the monetary gold reserves and resources of our own nation. The two do not work together. Either we shipped that gold abroad foolishly or we had to ship it abroad because we did not have available foreign paper currencies convertible into American money with which to liquidate the obligations that were currently due during the year in which the gold (payments were madle. I do not think there is anybody in this country who can say whether our adverse balance of trade was not more, and considerably more, last year than $200,000,000, and when we shipped that gold abroad we shipped it abroad as at least 12739-227
an indication of the minimum of our foreign unfavourable balance of trade.
I do not know all that must be done but I believe that we should make some attempt to set up a monetary system with wide control under which we can balance not only the national budget but provincial budgets and municipal budgets as well because I do not think it is going to accomplish very much to balance the national budget if provincial and municipal governments are going to continue to face bankruptcy. I think budgets should be balanced and I also think debts should be properly serviced. I believe that we should command the respect of the financial communities and the lenders, but I also believe that we should respect the confidence of the *taxpayer. If we can hold the confidence of lenders only by sacrificing the wealth of taxpayers through confiscatory taxation, then I am afraid the confidence of the lenders is going to be of very little value to this nation.
I believe, in addition, that we should be able to finance the construction of those things which will add to the national revenue. I believe that our great tourist resources in the maritime provinces, in Quebec, in Ontario and in the west should be developed as a means of inducing Americans to exchange for Canadian goods and services American dollars, and in addition, I believe that we should be able to finance the development of our resources and the maintenance of law and order so that those in the United States and elsewhere who can afford to live in a country in which they would prefer to bring up their families will come to Canada and settle and bring their wealth to us.
That is one way in which I believe we can meet a foreign exchange situation that will always confront the Dominion of Canada. The moment we get prosperous one of our most difficult problems in international exchange is going to be how to prevent our Canadians in such times from going south of the line in the winter time and to the attractions which the Americans present and spending more of Canadian currency in the American tourist trade than the American tourists are spending with us. I do not believe that the Americans should be exploited, but I do feel there is much we can do in the way of an intelligent administration of currency and credit to put our own people to work developing honest attractions that will bring about a movement northward in the summer time that will affect our movement southward in the winter. In that way I believe we can use the national currency and credit to increase the security of the unit of exchange abroad.

Bank oj Canada

More than that. I believe that we must rehabilitate our railroad systems. We cannot afford to allow the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific railway systems to operate in competition with the magnificent roads that are operating now in the United States without assisting our railways to bring their road beds, their equipment and their time schedules up to the transcontinental standards now in operation south of the line. These things can all be done. We can do what New Zealand is doing. New Zealand has now gone forward, after years of bonusing and building up her foreign trade in butter, to set up an agricultural governmental institution wherein all of her agricultural products are going to be taken over at a price, and then are going to be bartered for the things which the government of New Zealand feels it can secure for the benefit of the people of that country. We cannot progress in Canada unless we are prepared to raise the standiard1 of living of the farmers of western Canada to the same level that obtains for our governmental employees and for the people in our cities and industrial communities.
Yes, these things can be done, but they require a great deal of work, a great deal of courage, and a great deal of attention, and attempts to bring them about will not be perfect at their inception. While I am quite aware that monetary reform is not the whole answer; that it is merely one step, I do suggest, however, that if a properly constituted national bank were created1 that would operate as a public utility issuing currency and credit in terms of public need, many of the political, economic and social problems which now seem to be insurmountable would, I believe, fall well within the limits of practical administration.
We should I agree, assume that because certain institutions have been sanctified in the past they should be changed only with care and caution, but I think, now that we are well advanced into the new era, what we are asking the government to do in making the Bank of Canada a national institution is only whait other nations have found by experience to be a sound and1 necessary thing to do. If I can read reports at all I think the principle of public ownership for the Bank of Canada was recommended by Mr. Leman, Sdr Thomas White and Mr. Brownlee who constituted a majority of the Canadian Macmillan Commission. That is so because the cost of public finance must be reduced through the issue of currency as a state function. That conclusion is in line with the following passage of the English Macmillan report:

The greatest difficulty, however, which we foresee is the fulfilment of the second task, namely, to remedy the shortage of definitely sound borrowers for the purpose of new enterprise. The vicious circle is complete. The decline of new enterprise has reacted adversely on profits and prices, and the low level of profits and prices stands in the way of new enterprise. It is for this reason that some of us think that in the domestic field it may be necessary to invoke governmental enterprise to break the vicious circle. In the international field measures of an analogous kind would have to take a somewhat different form. In this ease also the vicious circle is complete. The unwillingness to lend, coupled with the frequently unwise use of borrowed funds, has destroyed the credit of borrowers, which reinforces the unwillingness to lend. In many cases, no single creditor is ready to take the risk which is absolutely required in the interest of creditors as a whole, since this report was written. ,
In Great Britain they have gone into public spending; in the United States and Australia they have also gone into public spending, and as a result confidence has been restored and private enterprise is again beginning to move. If we had the courage to take over the Bank of Canada and to put the necessary medium of exchange into circulation through the proper employment of men engaged in public works, social services and public enterprises, we shall soon find that we have restored the circulation of consumers' buying power and created an effective demand which will inspire private enterprise to go to work. But until we do that we are going to slough along, picking up only the crumbs that fall from the tables of other countries where expansion and public work is going forward, and doing nothing to secure for our own people those great benefits which have come to the people of other nations through governmental action.
I do not for one moment think the tasks are simple, but I do think there is plenty of reason now for parliament to set up the machinery and to engage the best, most competent men available to carry out the work parliament wishes to see done; that is, to put the people to work creating and distributing wealth, so that the cultural heritage of mankind can be placed on a higher standard than it enjoys to-day. I think every man in this chamber is imbued with that desire just as much as I am, possibly, in some cases, even more, and that is why I say that this is the paramount political issue of to-day. It is above party politics and calls upon men of all parties, in the commons, in the senate, and in business, to unite to stabilize our finance so that our social and economic security may be restored.
Now let me say this; I know it is easy to say, "Oh, I don't know anything about finance.

It is above me. It is a highly complex problem. It is an academic issue." I think many are beginning to realize that Keynes of Cambridge has performed a great service to the academic world by writing his book A General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money.

speechtext:
In speaking on this Bank of Canada bill the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard brought in the chartered banks to a great extent and gave some figures in respect to them that are not correct. On page 3331 of Hansard1 he is reported1 as saying:
I have checked the figures and I find that in 1934, on a capital investment of $144,000,000, the banks made an actual profit of $18,000,000 which figures out roughly to twelve per cent- not bad for a depression year.
In the first place the hon. member has not added the rest account to the capital. Instead of $144,000,000 invested it was $276,000,000, a difference of some forty-eight per cent. Then, where he said that the banks made an actual profit of $18,000,000, that is before deducting the taxes and other things which had to come out of it, so that the actual return on that capital investment, instead of being, as he states, some twelve per cent, is only some four and a half per cent.
Then he goes on to say:
... profit was paid out by the Bank of Montreal at the rate of eight per cent-The other
banks ranged from six per cent to twelve per cent, but the average stood at about twelve per cent.
How could figures from six to twelve average twelve? So the hon. member is wrong in that respect. Then he goes on to say:
-then they put aside as rest account an amount almost as great.
That is referring to the year 1934. But in fact none of the banks put any amount in the rest account at all; they have not put anything into rest or reserve for several years. In fact they have lost some of their reserves during these years of stress. Surely we are entitled to have a fair report about these banks.
Then the hon. member goes on to say:
Last year, in 1935, their profits were a little better, and the preliminary dividend paid by the Bank of Montreal in the first quarter of this year, 1936, is, I believe, four per cent.
Well, to be accurate, it was two per cent, or rather 3-75 per cent per annum on the total capital employed, rest and reserve. It might be said that the rest is not port of the capital, but it was largely provided by the shareholders as part of the capital of the banks. In many cases they issued their stock at a premium of 100 per cent and added that premium to their rest. So that sum was mostly provided by the stockholders.

It is, therefore, fair to correct the hon. member's figures in these respects; that is instead of $144,000,000 being the capital invested they had $276,000,000, a mistake on the part of the hon. member of some forty-eight per cent. When he referred to the banks having made $18,000,000 profit he figured that before taking off taxes, pension fund and other deductions, a mistake there of some thirty per cent. When he says that the dividend figures range from six to twelve per cent and calls that an average of twelve per cent he makes a mistake of some twenty-five per cent. When he says that they put aside as rest account an amount almost as great, the fact is that they did not put anything aside for rest account, so there he makes a mistake beyond measurement in percentage. When he says that the Bank of Montreal in the first quarter of 1936 paid four per cent when they paid only two per cent or rather at the rate of 3-75 per cent per annum on their actual capital he made another mistake of some fifty per cent. So in those few lines we find five mistakes, on the average fifty per cent wrong. If in respect to other things which he has stated before this committee the hon. member is as wrong as in these to which I have called attention, how much dependence can this committee place upon his statements?
We know that the chartered banks have been the bulwark of the financial system of this country, and they should be treated fairly. They are regulated by this parliament, and surely it is unfair that a wrong impression should be given about their earnings, which earnings are as small as is safe under the conditions under which they operate. I think it is only fair that these corrections should be put upon Hansard, because I have looked up the figures from the bank returns and I assure my hon. friend that they are in accordance with the facts.

subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OP CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
The amendment
before us may be some slight improvement, but I submit that it will not enable the Bank of Canada to perform the functions which the Bank of Canada should perform. Again I believe that the government in introducing a measure of this kind is not keeping faith with the electorate who sent them to power. Reference has already been made in this parliament to the address of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) on the night of the general election, October 14, 1935. On that occasion he said:
The election is an endorsation of the Liberal view that credit is a public matter not of interest to bankers only but of direct concern to every citizen.
I heartily concur in the latter part of that statement. I hoped that that might be the

Bank of Canada
Liberal view. But under this legislation credit does not become a public matter; credit still remains under private control. We shall never have credit fully a public matter until the government of this country is prepared to take over not merely the central bank but the chartered banks as well. However I quite admit that a properly constituted and controlled central bank may have a very great effect in the control of credit. We argued for such a bank yearns ago. Two yearns ago when the Conservative government introduced the Bank of Canada Act we supported it, not because we liked the private control, which we believed the act maintained, but because we believed in the principle of a central bank and we thought the Bank of Canada Act was one step in the right direction. The Liberals at that time refused to have anything to do with the central bank as then constituted; they criticized it most severely, put themselves on record as opposed to it and pleaded for a publicly controlled bank. Yet now they introduce legislation which, as I said when the resolution was under discussion, does not implement the statements that were made on behalf of the Liberal party from one end of this country to the other. I repeat: On the eve of an election the Prime Minister said that credit is a public matter. The legislation now before us and the directorate we are setting up does not ensure that even the control of credit will be a public matter. We are setting up a private bank or, if we may so describe it, a hybrid institution, half public and half private.
The present Prime Minister went on to say:
It is a verdict against a privately owned and controlled central bank.
Undoubtedly, as it has existed so far, the bank has been privately owned and controlled, but I suggest that the bank we are to have after this measure is passed will not be publicly owned and controlled. It is not fair to permit the impression to go out that we believe the bank which we shall have as a result of this bill is going to merit that designation. or that in this legislation the government is making good its pledges to the people.
I propose to vote for the measure; what else can I do? It may be a slight improvement over what we had before. We believed that the setting up of a central bank, even as it existed previously, was an improvement on no central bank. However this measure is not what we are after. As I shall try to point out later in my observations, this bank in my judgment will not fulfil the function a central bank ought to fulfil.
The Prime Minister said:
It is a verdict in favour of a properly constituted national bank to perform the functions of rediscount and the control of currency issue considered in terms of public need.
There is nothing in this legislation, as has been pointed out by the hon. member for Van-couver-Burrard (Mr. McGeer), which would seem to suggest that the bank is to be given control in order that it may function in terms of public need. That is a point which ought to be driven home upon the people of Canada. The Prime Minister went on to say:
There can be no mistaking the demand for a restoration to the government of Canada of control over credit and currency issue.
It is for government control over credit and currency issue that a good many of us have been pleading for years. But this measure does not give it. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) cannot say that this measure gives government control over credit and currency issue. In this instance the government passes over its control to another body, on which it is merely represented. That is not government control. Only recently in railway matters we have got rid of a board of trustees in order that we may more effectively bring the railways under public control, and to do that we are now setting up a board of directors. Even under the new arrangement the railway does not come immediately and directly under departmental control. This Liberal government protested against the old arrangement in railway matters in that such an arrangement set up a body the government could not control. Now, in the present instance, in this central bank legislation, the government is setting up another body which it does not control. There is no use blinking that fact; the government does not control the Bank of Canada. It simply has certain representatives on the board.

The Prime Minister's statement refers to issuing. We have witnessed just now a first-class example of the way in which we play around words. The right hon. gentleman refers to credit and currency issue, not control. I take it that the issue of currency ought never to be given to any other body. Some years ago we had one dollar and two dollar bills on which appeared the king's head, and we had five dollar and ten dollar bills and higher on which appeared the heads of the presidents of the various banks which issued paper money. I said that I hoped the time would come when the king's head would be placed on every piece of money issued in Canada. But we are not putting the king's head on the Bank of Canada bills; we are putting on them the head of t'he president of the Bank of Canada. The money is not issued by the government. In fact, the impression has been given that it would not be safe to entrust a government with issuing its own currency. I am not saying whether or not that is so, but I say that immediately after the election the Prime Minister said:
There can be no mistaking the demand for a restoration to the government of Canada of control over credit and currency issue.

speechtext:
I will leave the Prime Minister to answer that question. He is an adept at giving definitions. Perhaps he would answer it to-night. He proceeds:
As the campaign proceeded, the issue of control, by the people, of all functions of government, through their representatives in arliament, and not by any other power, ecame increasingly clear.
One of the functions of government is that of issuing money. According to the Prime Minister that function was to be in the hands of parliament. It is not placed in the hands of parliament by this legislation. I would have been content if we had set up a board directly under control of parliament, but we have not done that. The Prime Minister concludes:

The electorate has declared that a responsible ministry, not organized finance and international money power, is to control in all matters of state.
Well, he may reply that under this measure there is control by the responsible ministry, but he shares that control with the financial powers. As I study this legislation-and I have been trying to read something of the history of central banks-I believe that a central bank can perform its functions only as it is independent of business pressure. Wre know how the present board' of directors of the Bank of Canada was selected. The chamber of commerce put up a slate. It is quite true there was a wide distribution of the shares, but as everybody knows shareholders cannot be got together easily, and for that reason the chamber of commerce put over a slate on which business men predominated. It may be said that we have a farmer on the board; yes, but he does not act as a farmers' representative. As my colleague points out, many of the directors were strictly financial people directly concerned in other financial matters.
If I understand aright, one of the main functions of a central bank is to maintain general price levels. It can do that more or less by restricting or expanding credit. The central bank is required to do the very thing that is unpopular at a given time. It must expand when there is a tendency to contract, and it must contract when there is overexpansion. Do we think it is possible for men trained in business, and having outside business interests, to perform that function? I believe that is one of the weaknesses of the old board. We did not get an independent board, but rather a board of business men who looked at the matter from a financial standpoint.
We now have provision for some government appointees. I cannot say who will be appointed, but if I were a betting man I would be willing to wager quite a sum that we would have the same class of people put on the board to represent the government. That has been the history in the past, whether Conservatives or Liberals were in power. We shall have financial men put on that, board. Of course, there will be one or two others to give colour to the idea that it represents all classes, but it will be a board essentially dominated by the present financial interests. Just recently we had the nationalization of the central bank of Denmark. The legislation by which that bank was nationalized provided that no directors might be directors or managers of any private undertaking. Just let me put this to the Prime

Bank oj Canada
Minister: If he wants his board, poorly instituted as it is, to be thoroughly free from business influences, will he place on this board no one who is connected with private undertakings? Dare he do that?

subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OP CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext: I said that I resented the idea that one dealing with private interests was necessarily dishonest.

subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OP CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
That is not my implication, and it never was. I do not for one minute hold that all men in private enterprise are crooks or anything of the kind. I can well agree with the Prime Minister that a great many of them are actuated by very high motives. I am not suggesting anything else and the Prime Minister is not going to divert me from my argument. I do say, and I have felt for a long time, that directors of chartered 'banks ought not to be interested in other private concerns. That is my opinion with regard to that phase of the question. I .taught school out in the west forty years ago and I can remember the instance of a man who had timberland and who was delivering wood to the school, who was not eligible as a trustee. The idea was not that all men who teamed wood were cranks
or crooks; the idea was that if a man was to be independent as a trustee he ought not to be mixed up with many other things. That idea is carried out in a great many departments of public life. I should like to see the time come when a man could not be a director of a chartered bank when he was director of a number of other private concerns. That is all. I am not attacking the probity of these men, but at the same time I do not think they are angels. I do not think they are exempt from the weakness of other human beings.
I come now to the directorate of this central bank. This directorate ought to be able on occasion, and especially at a time of crisis, to go directly counter to prevailing financial opinion. A board of directors selected from those who are interested in financial undertakings is not likely to do that. That is all I am trying to say and the Prime Minister need not try to divert me. I said with regard to the bank of Denmark, that in that legislation the directors of the new bank were not to be directors or managers of any private undertaking. I said to the Prime Minister-and I say it again-.that I could not imagine his putting such legislation upon the statute books of Canada.
I believe that the issuance of currency and the control of credit should be a state function. I agree largely with the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. McGeer), although I do not know that I can follow him in all details. When he was speaking yesterday the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) asked him whether he thought he could create something of value out of nothing. That was another of those little remarks which are thrown in and which may so easily mislead the public. I should like to quote from an address made by the hon. member before the Canadian Club in Toronto on November 13, 1933, when he was Secretary of State. This is contained in a pamphlet entitled The Depression, Its Monetary Problems. I should like to answer the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George with his own words. He said:
The prevalent conception that bank deposits may only be created by actual deposits of specie, or its equivalent in dominion notes or foreign exchange, is quite erroneous.
I think that is what the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard was trying to say. The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George gave certain figures as of that date three years ago, and went on to say:
The credit extended by the Canadian banks is secured in less than one-fourth part by the capital and surplus of the banks, but largely
Bank of Canada

by the good faith, property, administrative efficiency and business capacity of the customers to whom such loans are made.

The Minister of Finance says that that is right, and I believe that he is in sympathy with a good deal of it. The former Secretary of State continued:
The aggregate of these loans, by which the bulk of all deposits are created, largely represents advances of credit made by the banks to their customers.
That is the very thing which many of us seem to find it so difficult to get into our heads. Every loan creates a deposit. Again and again it has been said on the floor of this chamber that the banks are simply lending out savings deposits. The word "savings" is not always used, but the idea is that the loans are deposits-real money-placed at the disposal of the banks by their customers. The hon. gentleman continued:
In more modern times the invention and adoption of the cheque system has effected a radical revolution in monetary policy. The cheque has now largely usurped the function of metallic coins and government notes as currency.
After reviewing some monetary history, he went on to say:
The result is that, in modern practice, seventy to eighty per cent of the aggregate of all deposits, shown in the Canadian bank returns, represent in reality the amount of loans made by the banks and then outstanding.
In order that there might be no mistake about his meaning, he said later on:
The cheque system, which has been developed, enables the banks to create-
"Create" was the word he used.
-money without the issue of their printed notes.
Last night the hon. member suggested that only the creator could create something out of nothing, but in that case he used the very word "create." He continued:
But the cheque system, which now prevails, enables the banks, as I have stated, to create credit money at will for many hundreds of millions of dollars in excess of their note issues. $1,428,000,000 of such credit money was issued and outstanding on September 30 last. In comparison with this bank credit money, the amount of all other money in circulation is quite insignificant.
One more paragraph of the same kind:
The fact remains, however, that the banks now have an almost complete monopoly of the credit facilities of the country. They may restrict or extend credit at will within the limitations which I have mentioned; and the question has arisen whether the control of credit should continue to be exercised in the sole discretion of the directors and officials of the banks.

Without going into the theory of the matter, I think I will just leave that statement of the former Secretary of State to speak for itself. In brief, what is the situation that we have before us? In the Bank of Canada, it has been pretty clearly recognized, there is no need of capital, and yet this government is proceeding to extend the capital of the bank. Under the present arrangements a few shareholders

that is, few in comparison with all the citizens of Canada-are given certain guaranteed profits. I do not know why it is that a few people should have 4J per cent while, if I want to put my savings into one of the chartered banks to-day, I can receive only 14 per cent. A comparatively few favoured people who are in that happy position can have guaranteed profits. Further, the business interests are able, as I have said, to elect a slate of directors, and they will have a very considerable influence, I fancy, on the new board, though I agree to a considerable extent with the hon. member (Mr. McGeer) that the directors may not be as important as the executive committee. In any case, the business interests, it seems to me, will be dominant in the new set-up, and this strikes me as a surrender of the sovereignty of government in that field. The hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard was speaking of what had been accomplished in various countries by utilizing money to supply the needs of the people. I should like to read one or two paragraphs from an interesting article that appeared in the May-June number of International Affairs, which most hon. members know is the organ of the Royal Institute of International Affairs. The article is by the Right Hon. Lord Passfield, on Soviet Communism, Its Present Position and Prospects. Dealing with currency matters, he says, at page 403:
To the bolsheviks, currency, whether in the form of money or of bank credit, is merely an inanimate slave of the community, or shall we say a tool, like the immense park of hundreds of thousands of tractors, available for use here or there on the quarter of a million collective or state farms. The tool dictates nothing. It is merely an expedient for giving freedom of choice to all the several consumers and producers, as an alternative to supplying them all with definite rations, whether they like them or not. Hence currency is created, just as are postage stamps, to whatever extent is found to be required for the purpose of the people, quite without influence on the projected aggregate total of commodities and services, or of the amount of trade. As prices are, for the most part, fixed by the various organs of government, and fixed not on cost alone but on a whole range of considerations of public benefit, an increase or a decrease of currency has no effect on these prices. If the currency seems, at any moment, to be inconveniently deficient, more is provided by a stroke of the

Bank of Canada
pen. If there seems to be more in circulation than is comfortable, the issue of further paper roubles or bank credit is' suspended, or, by means of propaganda for an internal loan, essentially a voluntary determent of the expenditure of wages or other incomes, a large block of currency is withdrawn from circulation. The monetary quantity of currency in circulation has absolutely no influence on the aggregate volume of employment or of consumption, or on the quantity or kind of production that is planned and undertaken. Moreover, by the simple expedient of prohibiting any import or export of Soviet currency, which accordingly never passes the frontier in either direction, and by making all foreign trade, including the import or export of gold and silver, a government monopoly, all the complications of international rates of exchange are avoided.
A little later on he says:
Low prices of manufactures abroad exert no influence on prices in the U.S.S.R., they are only an advantage to the soviet commissar for foreign trade, and not a disadvantage to the soviet producer, whose earnings remain unchanged whatever may be the commodities that it suits the soviet union to purchase abroad or to export in order to pay for its purchases. What future bolshevik students will say, when one day they turn over the hundreds of thousands of books and pamphlets about currency that cumber the British Museum, I simply cannot imagine.
I give that simply because of the remarkable development which has taken place in Russia. Soviet Russia after the war was a poverty stricken country. After the revolution they had practically no equipment for producing at least any of their heavier commodities. Everything had been disorganized by war and revolution. They obtained practically no outside credit, or very little. They were able to get a little, and for that they had to pay dearly by the export of commodities at a very low rate. But by some means or another-I do not profess to know how it was done-in the last ten years they have built up a wonderfully productive machine. I am not going to read any further from this article but I would commend it to the members of the committee. That Lord Passfield is a very careful investigator is well recognized by all students of economics. Well, what Russia did, they did with very little outside credit; and they are proceeding in an increasing degree to supply the material needs of their very large population.
Now, I ask, why it is that- we cannot utilize our currency and credit in some such manner as they have done in Russia in supplying the needs of the people? Again and again through these years we have considered in this house the matter of currency and credit and we still hold to the old theory. I cannot say tint I follow the theories of my friends to tie left. I for one do not believe
that we shall get out of the woods simply by printing more money. That is not what I am after; I do not think that is what is involved in monetary reform. But I say that our present system is piling up debt upon debt which we cannot pay. Our present system is failing to function in the interests of the masses of the people, and under those circumstances it seems to me that this parliament ought to listen to the plea which has been made by the hon. member for Van-couver-Burrard and not pass through these " particular pieces of legislation without considering the more fundamental problems involved. With regard to the bill that is before us, I am not allowed to move an amendment; I do not see how I can under the ruling given the other day. I have either to reject the bill or to vote for it. I suppose the only thing I can do under these circumstances is to vote for it, but I am absolutely dissatisfied with what the government has done in bringing in a measure of this kind. I do not think it is going to secure for the people of Canada what might be secured by a properly constituted and controlled central bank.

I am going to make one of my two minute speeches. I dislike this particular method of increasing government control. To me the issuing of fifty-one per cent of new stock, and an increase in the board, an additional four members to be appointed by the government, or, according to the amendment, six, smacks of big, and possibly what we have come to call, slick business methods. I do not think it is anything like as straightforward as buying out the original shares would have been, and when I remember
Bank of Canada

the speed with which the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) rose in his place in committee to try to head off the then member for Macleod in his attempt to move in committee for a government owned bank, it is really funny. I remember the zeal of the Liberals in castigating the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) and others who voted with him in supporting the central bank bill as brought down by the Conservative government then in power. Why, [DOT] this country simply rang with the condemnation of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation members for not voting for public ownership like the righteous Liberal party did. As a matter of fact, at that time, while I understood the motives of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and those associated with him, I did not support the central bank bill, not because I did not think it better than what we had, but because it was not all we wanted to have and I felt that the only way I could protest against the bill as it was was to vote against it. But what I felt about that bill was exactly what my colleagues in the southeast comer felt at that time.
What I would like to ask the Minister of National Defence is: Where is now all his zeal for a publicly owned bank? I remember how hard he worked at that time, and it does seems strange that he should have so completely changed his mind.
I think it would have been better to buy out all the original shares but, to express myself exactly, we never needed to sell shares of the central bank. Did anyone ever hear of anybody drilling for a well with the hope of striking a spring and then pouring down into the well five million gallons of water that it might mix with the spring water before it was drawn up again, or did anyone ever hear of anybody opening up a coal mine and then taking down five million tons of coal to bring it back up again? The business of the central bank was to create currency and credit, and for the life of me I have never been able to see why we have to go to the trouble of getting money to start with. But then, of course, I am not supposed to understand finance; it is so evidently a very deep subject.
I do not wonder that the Liberal government feel a bit jittery on this question, since this bill falls so far short of the promises they so definitely made during the campaign; then, too, the private members behind the government are not feeling comfortable about the matter as is evident to anybody who has had experience in parliament or has ever seen one before. I think the Finance minister, and the Prime Minister as well, must know by now that their followers are not content with

So I feel that I am standing for the principle by which I stood before when I say that I shall vote against this bill, not because it is not slightly better, but because I dislike the way in which it is being made better, and because I feel that it falls short of the promises which were made by the Liberal government during the campaign and that it is a betrayal of the confidence of the electorate.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, if I might repeat the remarks which I had to make on Keynes' book I should like to quote a paragraph which should commend itself to every student of this problem. He continues his reference to academical schools of economy by saying:
Our criticism of the accepted classical theory of economics has consisted not so much in finding logical flaws in its analysis as in pointing out that its tacit assumptions are seldom or never satisfied, with the result that it cannot solve the economic problems of the actual world.
That is exactly our problem to-day. In other words, while we are going ahead with an assumed increase in the government's control over the Bank of Canada, we are doing this by changing a board of directors that really does not exercise actual control over the administration of the bank's affairs. In other words, we are continuing the Bank of Canada as it was set up by the leader of the opposition and by the government that he led in the last House of Commons. There is no fundamental change in the Bank of Canada, or in the methods under which it is going to operate, or in the control that is actually exercised by the executive committee with wdiich his legislation vested the absolute control of the bank.

subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OP CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS

speechtext: No, no.

The governor in council
can appoint them, but under the act they are appointed to hold office for seven years

subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OP CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext: I am talking about the veto power.

subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OP CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
The only veto power that comes in is an extension of the veto power in the governor in council over the acts of the governor of the bank. If the governor of the bank refuses to agree in the decision of the executive committee-

Bank of Canada

subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OP CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext: Or the board.

subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OP CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
-or the board, then he must report that to the governor in council, but the only power the governor in council then has is to affirm or deny the action of the governor of the hank. The governor in council cannot, under any section of the act that I know of, say to the governor of the bank, you must do this, and make the governor of the bank carry it out. It is not within the power of the governor in council to say to the governor of the bank: Here is the policy of parliament to which we wish you to conform, and you must carry this out. But they can, under the present act, after calling parliament together and saying that the governor will not carry out the wishes of parliament, ask parliament to dismiss the governor and then they can put in a new governor who will carry out their policy. The board of directors of the bank have nothing more to say in the administration of the bank's affairs than the shareholders who own the stock of a company have in the administration of its affairs, and that is absolutely nothing. The board of directors is purely a group of men who sit in at the board and confirm very largely what the executive committee has done, because they are never in a position to do otherwise.
Now with reference to the suggestion as to what should be done, I think possibly we may find some instance in which Keynes may have changed his conclusions. I do not think however that he has ever changed any conclusions that he has held upon fundamental principles of monetary policy. He says:
The outstanding faults of the economic society in which we live are its failure to provide for full employment and its arbitrary and inequitable distribution of wealth and incomes.
He goes on to the question of creating an effective demand so that the available supply may be absorbed, and then he deals with the rate of interest and says that the rate of interest is bound to come down. He says:
The justification for a moderately high rate of interest has been found hitherto in the necessity of providing a sufficient inducement to save. But we have shown that the extent of effective saving is necessarily determined by the scale of investment and that the scale of investment is promoted by a low rate of interest.
There can be no doubt that this criterion will lead to a much lower rates of interest than has ruled hitherto; and, so far as one can guess at the schedules of the marginal efficiency of capital corresponding to increasing amounts of capital, the rate of interest is likely to fall steadily.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OP CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
It will be observed that
he uses the word "guess."

subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OP CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
No one can tell for certain what is going to happen in the future. He goes on to say:
But whilst there may be intrinsic reasons for the scarcity of land, there are no intrinsic reasons for the scarcity of capital.
And certainly the actions of Russia, Japan, the Roosevelt administration and Great Britain, prove that that is true. He goes on to say:
An intrinsic reason for such scarcity, in the sense of a genuine sacrifice which could only be called forth by the offer of a reward in the shape of interest, would not exist, in the long run-
-If, as he says in another section in the book, a central bank is created.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OP CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext: I think my hon. friend should quote that exactly.

subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OP CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
I shall be very glad to do so:
There can be no doubt that this criterion will lead to a much lower rate of interest than has ruled hitherto and, so far as one can guess at the schedules of the marginal efficiency of capital corresponding to increasing amounts of capital, the rate of interest is likely to fall steadily, if it should be practicable to maintain conditions of more or less continuous full employment-
How does he say you are going to maintain conditions of more or less continuous full employment? He deals with that in a very trite, Keynes' way of argument:
Unemployment develops, that is to say, because people want the moon; men cannot be employed when the object of desire (i.e. money) is something which cannot be produced and the demand for which cannot be readily choked off. There is no remedy but to persuade the public-
-that money can be created simply through a central bank.
I may be wrong; I may be presuming a great deal to offer a suggestion as to what this book really contains, because I think it is a book written not for men like myself or for the public but very largely for classical economists who have academic training. But he has pointed out certain things to the classical economists with academic training, whom we have long followed in their teachings. I think Ricardo and Pigou of recent times probably have had more influence upon the political economy of Great Britain than political leaders have exercised. We have accepted the teachings of Ricardo. In this book Keynes comes forward' to change the academic and classical economist into one who forces himself to make his theories find the sanction of actual experience, to make his theories stand
Bank of Canada

up under the test of practical political experience. In other words Keynes has taken what we call unorthodox economy and put it into this book in a classical version.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OP CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext: He says that the book is largely written for economists.

subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OP CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext: I think so. I have read it and studied it, and I am trying to give what I think is a layman's interpretation of its practical value and application. I do not know that one needs to stress the point that the Macmillan commission agreed upon unanimously, namely that the creation of currency and credit, the issue of currency and credit, the regulation of prices, the stabilization of production and all those factors that must be taken into consideration as well as money, must come under the control of men of unchallengeable independence. I agree that it is easy to say that our bank directors should be men of business experience; that is true. But they should be men of unchallengeable independence, having no other interest than the well-being of the community at large.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OP CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman answer a question? How does he reconcile that with government control?

subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OP CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext: The government control I should like to see established is something like the government control that we exercise over the supreme court. We would not think of allowing the members of our county courts, our provincial supreme courts or the Supreme Court of Canada to have any other interest during their active service than the well-being of the public and the nation.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OP CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext: But they frequently decide against the government.

subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OP CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext: There is no question as to that, but it is only in the determination of issues in accordance with the laws which are established. It cannot be helped that the government and the supreme court may conflict, as has occurred recently in the United States, but there is no reason why the course followed by the government of Canada could not have been followed by the government of the United States, so that the questions would have been sent to the Supreme Court of the United States for determination before being acted upon by the government.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OP CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext: Their constitution forbids that.

subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OP CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
But they could change their constitution in that regard, and in the light of the experience of the past year possibly the necessity of working out some arrangement by which the supreme court and the

government of the United States can work in harmony will be recognized and such an arrangement will be developed. In any event we have not that situation, in the Dominion of Canada. I think it is extremely rare that there has been any suggestion that the interpretations of our laws were violations of the general spirit of democratic government as we have it in this house. I do not think we have ever had any criticisms as to that. I quite appreciate that the board of directors of the Bank of Canada have no easy task, but what I say is that there is no reason for believing that such a board of a publicly owned bank and the government cannot work together in circulating and in regulating the circulation of the medium of exchange which constitutes the economic blood stream of our whole social order. Just because these problems are difficult is no reason for not undertaking them, and when there is opportunity for us to take another step forward, if it is necessary to change stagnation in business into activity, unemployment into employment and to advance the standard of living and the spread of culture, it is well worth the risk.
I may be criticized for expressing my views so keenly, but in connection with this great subject I feel that every man in public life should be at least willing to study this question, to formulate some definite ideas and to bring them into the council chamber of the nation for discussion. It is not necessary that they be adopted; even if they only promote intelligent discussion and intelligent pursuit of information that will lead to some effective solution of the great problems which governments have before them, it will be worth while. This, I think, is the greatest political issue and the greatest economic problem before us for solution, and until we solve it we cannot find the way to that social and economic security which we are all anxious to see everyone enjoy. The right hon. Prime Minister has said:
... once a nation parts with the control of its currency and credit, it matters not who makes the nation's laws. Usury, once in control, will wreck any nation. Until the control of the issue of currency and credit is restored to government and recognized as its most conspicuous and sacred responsibility, all talk of the sovereignty of parliament and of democracy is idle and futile. Those are strong words; they constitute a strong argument, and they are words of which this house ought to take full acount before it is too late.
Again, during the same debate, the right hon. gentleman said:
The hon. member for Vancouver Centre has referred already to what I said when speaking in this house on February 27, 1933, in outlining the position of the Liberal party on the central bank. I should like to read again the words

Bank oj Canada
quoted by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre. Referring to the control of credit and stating the position of the party with respect to the control of credit, I said:
"The Liberal party believes that credit is a public matter, not of interest to bankers only but of direct concern to the average citizen. It stands for the immediate establishment of a properly constituted national central bank, to perform the functions of rediscount and the control of currency issue, considered in terms of public need. A central bank is necessary to determine the supply of currency in relation to the domestic, social and industrial require* ments of the Canadian pepole; and also to deal with the problems of international commerce and exchange."
I desire to direct special attention to the words: "a properly constituted national central bank." Also:
To perform the functions of rediscount, and the control of currency issue, considered in terms of public need.
Note that the Prime Minister said, "in terms of public need," not private gain.
The acknowledgment of the Prime Minister that the sovereignty of parliament and democracy is dependent upon the recognition that the issue of currency and credit is the most conspicuous and sacred responsibility of government constitutes a clear repudiation of the views of orthodox finance and classical economy which have prevailed in British countries during the last one hundred years.
The statement of the leader of the Liberal party should be recognized as the outstanding economic pronouncement made during the depression. I have formed this conclusion because I think that in the brief statement which I have quoted he was able clearly to define the primary cause of the economic disturbance and to indicate in specific terms the basis upon which may be developed a practical and enduring remedy.
Now, the fact that I have spoken strongly upon this issue does not mean that I am a rebel, or that I am inconsistent with the ideals or the practical workings of the Liberal party. I have formed my own ideas on this great public issue. I advocated them before the banking and commerce committee and was given a delightful welcome by the Liberal members of that committee when I came from Vancouver to appear before it. When I accepted a Liberal nomination I did so reserving to myself the right to stand upon the floor of this house and adtvooarte monetary reform as a non-partisan issue in which all should join and cooperate to find a solution of our financial and economic problems. I am not downhearted because the government in this first session have not gone as far as I would like to see them go. But I would have been false to my constituents if I had not stood up in my place here and done exactly what I promised to do if I was elected. I say this
to the government: You have started on the problem of setting up for the Canadian people a properly constituted bank. This is only the first session. With what is going to happen in the United States in the next few years, with what has happened in Great Britain, in South Africa, in New Zealand and in Australia, this government can and, I am confident, will go forward', in its own perhaps cautious way, less active than I think it ought to be, but nevertheless it will fulfil the promise and the philosophy which is expressed in the quotation from the Prime Minister's statement I have read and upon which the Liberal party went to the electors. I hope we shall be able in the next election to go to the country with the same statement, not as a promise then but as a pledge fulfilled.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OP CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
May I be allowed to speak? I might as well embark a little myself. The right hon. gentleman attracts the lightning to himself by the manner in which he is now treating me. I made no reference to him at all. The reference I made was to the functions of government as at present constituted, and the ever-increasing weight of responsibility which rests upon the governor general in council-meaning the government of the day-and a responsibility which I do not hesitate for a moment to say is fully up to the physical and nervous capacity of any man occupying a position in any government, under these conditions. The constant multiplication of functions is due to a change which has come about in the conception of governmental functions. They have been constantly widening for the last twenty years, and indeed I am one who thinks one of the problems we shall have to face in the not distant future is the problem of adjustment, and an adjustment which wil1 in some manner be consistent with out system of responsible government. It will have to be an adjustment of the load in a way which will ensure that members of governments will at least have time to think about the things they are supposed to deal with. I am thinking of any government under present conditions.
Here we undertake as a state responsibility a larger measure of concern with and control over the vital functions of currency and credit. Is it possible to put that function directly into the hands of members of the government, and expect them to discharge it, along with their other functions? Any thinking man must recognize that men must be set apart to execute these functions for the state. That is what we are trying to do in the present bill. We are trying to ensure that those men shall be men who have the confidence of the government of the day. We do not mean that they will be rubber stamps to express in every thought and action the views of the government. In the nature of things if they are the kind of men who must run to the Minister of Finance or the Prime Minister to ask what shall be done in connection with every day to day function of banking, the government might just as well try to discharge the function through its own corporate entity. We must have men in whom the government has confidence, from the point of view of knowledge held by the government respecting the general views of the individual with respect to policy. There must be knowledge on the part of the govern-
Questions

ment that the individual holds views with respect to the matter he is to administer which are in harmony with the views of the government, and that his conduct will at all times be assured on major matters. That is the attitude I take of the executive functions. But I also hold the opinion, in contradiction of those expressed in other quarters, that the executive committee of the bank cannot continue to carry out between sessions of the board of governors or board of directors policies contrary to the expressed views of that board of directors. If that were attempted, I believe an utterly impossible situation would be created.
